extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, and readers interested in political economy and public policy
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of corn trade and bounties
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and descriptive principles about bounties, drawbacks, premiums, and the structure and regulation of the corn trade (inland dealers, importers, exporters, carriers), arguing for free inland trade and criticising price controls and archaic statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties on manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: It can very seldom be reasonable to tax the industry of the great body of the people, in order to support that of some particular class of manufacturers; though if any particular manufacture were necessary for defence it might be vindicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounties might be defensible for defence-essential manufactures (examples: bounties upon exportation of British-made sail-cloth and gunpowder). Giving bounties in times of general difficulty is especially absurd; bounties are often expensive and can turn public wealth into folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawbacks vs bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: What is called a bounty is sometimes no more than a drawback, and consequently is not liable to the same objections as what is properly a bounty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customs distinction: drawbacks are allowances given upon goods exported in the same form in which they are imported; when the form is altered by manufacture they are called bounties. Examples: bounty on refined sugar as a drawback of duties on brown/Muscovado sugar; bounty on wrought silk as drawback of duties on raw silk; bounty on gunpowder as drawback of duties on brimstone and saltpetre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premiums to artists and manufacturers
rubrics_metrics.description: Premiums (public prizes) to artists and manufacturers who excel are not liable to the same objections as bounties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They encourage extraordinary dexterity and ingenuity, keep up emulation among workmen, do not divert significant capital to a single branch, and are trifling in expense compared to bounties. Their tendency is to perfect the work done in each occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties are costly and distortive
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of premiums is trifling, that of bounties very great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the bounty upon corn alone has sometimes cost the public, in one year, more than £300,000. Continued profusion of bounties in times of general difficulty is strongly criticized as absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of the corn trade
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade of the corn merchant is composed of four different branches: (1) the trade of the inland dealer; (2) the merchant-importer for home consumption; (3) the merchant-exporter of home produce for foreign consumption; and (4) the merchant-carrier, or the importer of corn in order to export it again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are distinct trades with different interests and effects on the home market; policy analysis should treat them separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest of the inland dealer aligns with public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest of the inland dealer and that of the great body of the people are, even in years of the greatest scarcity, exactly the same: he must raise the price only as the real scarcity requires and never beyond what is prudent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By raising price appropriately he discourages consumption and proportions supply to demand, avoiding famine; excessive raising risks leftover stock and loss; insufficient raising risks famine. The inland dealer’s knowledge of crops and sales enables him to judge proper proportioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inland dealers cannot practically monopolize corn
rubrics_metrics.description: It is scarce possible, even by the violence of law, to establish an extensive monopoly of corn; wherever trade is left free, corn is of all commodities the least liable to be engrossed or monopolised by a few large capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: the commodity's total value exceeds what a few private capitals can buy; production uses a great quantity of dispersed industry; first owners are scattered geographically, preventing concentration and general combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of dearths and famines
rubrics_metrics.description: A dearth never has arisen from any combination among inland dealers but from real scarcity, sometimes by waste of war but most commonly the fault of the seasons; a famine has usually arisen from violence of government attempting improper remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examination suggests government intervention (like price controls or restraints) is the principal cause turning dearths into famines, rather than merchant behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free inland trade as preventive of famine
rubrics_metrics.description: The unlimited, unrestrained freedom of the corn trade is the only effectual preventive of the miseries of a famine and the best palliative of the inconveniencies of a dearth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free trade allows division of scarce supplies across time and regions, mitigates season-to-season shortages, and should be fully protected by law because the trade is especially exposed to popular odium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government price controls cause harm
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government orders all dealers to sell their corn at what it supposes a reasonable price, it either hinders them from bringing it to market (producing famine) or encourages consumption so fast as to produce a famine before the season's end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price ceilings discourage supply or accelerate consumption; they are ineffective remedies for real scarcity and typically worsen outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular blame of corn merchants is misplaced and harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: In years of scarcity, inferior ranks impute distress to the avarice of the corn merchant, making him an object of hatred and danger; this popular odium drives respectable people away from the trade and leaves it to inferior dealers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The social consequences include risk of ruin, plunder of magazines, and a supply sector composed of less reputable participants, which harms overall provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancient laws against engrossing and forestalling were unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes (e.g., 5th and 6th of Edward VI cap. 14) enacted that buying corn to sell again should be reputed an unlawful engrosser with severe punishments, aiming to annihilate middlemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws attempted to force farmers to retail and to prevent middlemen from arising; they were violations of natural liberty and politically impolitic; later statutes softened these restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibiting manufacturers from retailing was misguided
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient policy often prohibited manufacturers from exercising the trade of a shopkeeper to protect a particular order (shopkeepers), but this violated natural liberty and was unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forcing division of capital or preventing a person from combining trades reduces efficiency: a manufacturer forced to retail withdraws capital from manufacture and cannot undercut vigilant shopkeepers because of divided capital and required profits on distinct capitals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcing farmers to act as corn merchants hinders cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: The law which obliged the farmer to carry on the trade of a corn merchant forced him to divide his capital and obstructed improvement and cultivation of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If farmers could sell their whole crop to corn merchants, their whole capital could return immediately to cultivation, supporting more cattle, servants, and improvements; compulsion to retail makes corn scarcer and dearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholesale dealers support production by providing market and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Wholesale dealers afford a ready market, take goods off producers' hands quickly, sometimes advance their price, and their capital supports many small producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: wholesale merchants support manufacturers as corn merchants could support farmers; this enables producers to keep capital employed where productive and mitigates losses from perishable commodities or price fluctuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charles II statute liberalised inland trade and aided tillage
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 15th of Charles II c.7 engrossing or buying of corn to resell (so long as price did not exceed certain thresholds) was declared lawful to many persons, and this statute contributed more to plentiful supply and increase of tillage than other laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute granted the inland trade much of the liberty and protection it enjoyed and helped lower corn prices prior to later bounties; the evolution of statutes shows gradual softening of earlier prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular fears of engrossing/forestalling are irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The popular fear of engrossing and forestalling may be compared to popular terrors and suspicions of witchcraft — unjustified and encouraged by legal restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoring freedom to inland trade would likely dispel these fears, as removing the enabling legal mechanism for accusations of malfeasance or conspiracy removed fear of witchcraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inland trade's primacy for home supply
rubrics_metrics.description: For supplying the home market the importance of the inland trade is vastly greater than that of importation or exportation (computed proportions given as illustrative: imports ~1/570 of consumption; exports ~1/31 of annual produce).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political arithmetic is only illustrative, but the point is that inland trade is the principal channel for home supply and deserves priority in policy consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of merchant-importers on money price and real value
rubrics_metrics.description: The merchant-importer of foreign corn for home consumption tends to lower the average money price of corn but not diminish its real value or the quantity of labour it can maintain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowering the money price raises the real value of silver, which lowers money prices of other commodities, enlarges the market for domestic industry, and tends to encourage cultivation; importation therefore benefits industry and home market in real terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import duties and price-triggered regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical statute example: by the 22d of Charles II c.13 the importation of wheat when home-market price did not exceed certain thresholds was subjected to duties (16s when <= 53s 4d; 8s when <= £4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates a regulatory mechanism where import taxation is tied to domestic price thresholds; such rules affect whether importation is effectively prohibited or allowed depending on domestic prices.
